title: VARCHAR Data Type
description: Learn how to use the VARCHAR data type to store variable-length, non-Unicode string data.

data.text: The VARCHAR data type stores variable-length, non-Unicode string data. Use VARCHAR when the data length varies from row to row.

data.title: VARCHAR Syntax
data.content: Defines a VARCHAR column with a specified length.

data.title: VARCHAR(max) Syntax
data.content: Defines a VARCHAR column with maximum storage of 2 GB.

data.text: n defines the string length from 1 to 8,000. If not specified, the default is 1. The storage size is the actual length of the data plus 2 bytes.

data.title: Create VARCHAR Column
data.content: Creates a table with a VARCHAR column and demonstrates insertion.

data.text: `VARCHAR(n)` stores the characters actually used plus two bytes of length information. Declaring more room than you use costs nothing on disk, so choose a length that reflects the real domain rather than the exact value. The script below compares CHAR with VARCHAR storage.

data.title: Compare CHAR and VARCHAR storage
data.content: The VARCHAR row stores only its four characters plus overhead; the CHAR row always stores the declared ten bytes.

data.title: The truncation trap
data.text: Inserting more characters than the column allows raises error 8152 (`String or binary data would be truncated`); SQL Server never silently trims. If the source field can grow, widen the column in advance — but be aware that `VARCHAR(max)` values above 8000 bytes are stored off-row and can cost an extra read.

data.title: Interview answer
data.text: Explain it plainly: CHAR is fixed-length and pads every value to the declared size; VARCHAR stores only the characters used plus a 2-byte length. Use VARCHAR for names, emails, and addresses; use CHAR only for genuinely fixed codes.

data.title: VARCHAR Key Points
points: VARCHAR stores variable-length, non-Unicode string data.
Length ranges from 1 to 8,000 characters; use VARCHAR(max) for up to 2 GB.
Storage size is actual length plus 2 bytes.
Use VARCHAR when data lengths vary across rows.
